60.story: A baggage check carries a donor’s initials and the name Chinook, Montana. The museum dates the gift to 14 May 1893 but cannot establish where Owney received it.
60.note: Chinook is the donor’s named town. Neither railway named on the tag appears to have passed through it. No map point is assigned.

84.story: A tag links Owney to the Lancaster House hotel. The catalog gives 5 May 1896, but its description also says the presentation date is unknown.
84.note: The date field and opening description give 5 May 1896; the same description then says the presentation date is unavailable. This conflicting record is shown as cataloged, not as a verified gift date.

92.story: Detroit’s shield-shaped tag advertised the “Beautiful City of the Straits.” The museum records it as a gift during Owney’s visit on 11 November 1893.

93.story: The workers who repaired mailbags and locks gave Owney this token. Their Washington shop returned around 200,000 repaired mailbags to service each month.

96.7.story: Letter carrier Sheldon E. Bovee gave Owney this leather baggage tag on 28 March 1892.

96.11.story: Postal clerks wrote “good luck to Owney” on a leather luggage tag. Their gift is dated 15 May 1896; the museum does not identify where they gave it to him.

99.story: Employees of the Railway Mail Service’s Third Division presented this badge-shaped token to their canine mascot on 18 April 1892.

103.story: Ainslie and Phyllis Carter gave Owney a tag marking his travels on a branch of the Cincinnati, Hamilton and Dayton railway.

106.story: Owney received this shield-shaped tag while visiting Nashville. It resembles a Railway Mail Service badge, but was made as a keepsake.

109.story: Postal clerk William Henry Gibbs Jr. and E. H. Dunning each inscribed a side of this tag. The museum associates the gift with a visit to Jackson.

110.story: F. M. Parker presented this horseshoe-shaped tag to “His Dogship.” Its reverse names a Railway Post Office car and gives the date 20 April 1892.
110.note: A railway service is identified, not a specific stop. No single city is plotted.

116.story: At their third national convention in Baltimore, members of the National Association of Post Office Clerks gave Owney a specially designed token.

117.story: A round brass tag records that Owney “called on” Dan Kelly’s grocery store on 22 June 1894.

120.story: Postal workers in Buffalo presented this round brass tag to Owney on 24 May 1893.

121.story: W. J. Tilley welcomed Owney aboard the Boston, Providence and New York City night mail train with this dated tag.
121.note: The train service is named; the place of exchange is not established. No single city is plotted.

124.story: An unnamed admirer engraved a short poem celebrating Owney’s visit to Haverhill, the “city of shoes.” The tag is dated 16 June 1894.

145.story: A hand-engraved tag marks Owney’s Seattle visit on 17 July 1895. Its donor is not identified.

148.story: Boston’s Railway Mail Service workers proclaimed themselves “First in Everything” on this tag, dated 27 April 1892.

150.story: The Washington city post office’s Registry Division gave Owney a badge-shaped token, made by local engraver William F. Lutz.

151.story: Railway mail clerk George W. Cooley gave Owney this token. It carries the date 19 March 1894.
151.note: The donor’s railway and the engraver’s city do not establish where the gift was received. No single city is plotted.

164.story: Owney received this tag while riding the Burlington and St. Louis portion of the Chicago, Burlington & Quincy Railroad.
164.note: A railway journey is identified, but the place of exchange is not. No single city is plotted.

199.story: Owney received this round metal tag aboard a Worcester and Norwich Railway Post Office car on 12 October 1894.
199.note: A train service is named, not a precise stop. No single city is plotted.

202.story: The museum identifies this as the first tag Owney received in Lancaster. Another tag connects him to the town two years later.

203.story: Postmaster Thomas E. Fletcher gave Owney this tag during the dog’s visit to Tilton on 2 May 1896.

207.story: A token from Woodbury’s in Boston offered Owney a 25-cent lunch. The gift is dated 27 April 1892.

210.story: A medal from Chicago’s World’s Columbian Exposition carries several donors’ names. The catalog dates it to 22 May 1893; the donors’ connection to Owney is unknown.

211.story: Nashville’s post office clerks gave Owney this tag on 9 April 1892. No individual donor is named.

216.story: Postal employees in the busy railway town of Corry presented this token to Owney on 26 May 1893.

219.story: Toledo’s produce exchange made Owney “our guest” with this promotional token, dated 26 March 1894.

229.story: Owney “stopped with Dick” at the Randolf Hotel, according to this token. It shares a date with the spoon bowl from Fort Wayne’s postal workers.

230.story: An admirer identified as L. March of New Richmond gave Owney this identification token. The date 12 September 1894 is engraved on it.

239.story: Postal clerk Fred S. White scratched his name into this decorative silver token for Owney. Its catalog date is 14 September 1894.

243.story: Duffy, Ferris and Spence, mounted collectors at Cincinnati’s post office, marked this rectangular tag with the date 6 September 1894.

368.story: Laconia postal clerk John O’Laughlin gave Owney this decorative token on 1 May 1896.

369.story: The Commercial Gazette, a Cincinnati newspaper, gave Owney this token on 12 April 1892. A local stamp cutter made it.

374.story: Clerks at Denver’s post office gave Owney this token on 13 August 1894, when roughly fifty clerks worked there.

376.story: The chief clerk of Philadelphia’s Railway Mail Service office gave Owney this token on 25 April 1892.

406.story: Owney received this token during an Athens visit on 17 September 1894. The museum’s description also connects him to nearby Logan the next day.

425.story: Hardware merchant Henry J. Bruner gave Owney an advertising token. Its date matches another gift from Kansas City’s postal clerks.

451.story: Plymouth postmaster William G. Hull gave Owney this tag. The museum interprets its marking “M. 5. 96.” as 5 May 1896.

453.story: Kansas City’s postal clerks gave Owney this token, produced by a local hardware company. It is dated 23 March 1894.

455.story: Taunton postal workers spelled their visitor’s name “Onee” on this tag, presented on 9 June 1894.

463.story: Railway mail clerks based in Portland gave Owney this token on a southbound mail car. They engraved their message over one face of a machinery company’s token.
463.note: Portland is the clerks’ base; the exchange took place on a train. No established stop is identified, so no map point is assigned.

475.story: Gunsmith John Koch of Rock Island gave Owney this identification token. His occupation and the date 9 May 1895 are marked on it.

481.story: Employees of Pierre’s small post office gave Owney this token. The museum catalogs it with the date 25 April 1896.
481.note: The Lawrence tag 482 has this same date, despite the distant cities. The records do not establish travel between them that day.

482.story: Pharmacist George Ketchum had this advertising token engraved “Presented to Owney,” with the date 25 April 1896.
482.note: The Pierre tag 481 has this same date, despite the distant cities. These are recorded dates, not evidence of a continuous itinerary.

488.story: This plate was fixed directly to Owney’s collar. It marks a Milwaukee encounter on 27 February 1896 and invites him to “call again.”

91.story: E. O. Atkinson and A. N. Trew gave Owney this token on 1 July 1895. It names both Calgary and Vancouver.
91.note: Two cities are named without resolving the place of exchange. No single location is plotted.

122.story: A triangular brass key connects Owney to Winona. The description records a date on its back: 16 June 1895.

153.story: This token resembles a postal cancellation, marking Owney as “received” in San Francisco at 3 a.m. on 12 April 1893.
153.note: The Cheyenne tag 457 is also described as received on 12 April 1893. The distant places expose a conflict in the records; their dates are preserved without inventing a route.

183.story: This copper tag names the Chicago and St. Louis Railway Post Office. The museum dates its presentation in Pontiac to 24 June 1895.

205.story: Scratched markings date this Hinton tag to 13 September 1894. Two sets of initials appear on the back, but their owners remain unidentified.

457.story: Cheyenne’s postal workers gave Owney a medal that advertised a different town: Gallatin, Montana. The museum dates the gift to 12 April 1893.
457.note: The San Francisco tag 153 has the same described gift date. The conflicting locations are kept visible as evidence limits, not joined into a claimed journey.
